items.stem: Under IAS 16, which cost should NOT be included in the initial cost of a machine?
options: Training staff to use the machine
items.answer: Training staff to use the machine
items.markingKey: Cost includes purchase price, duties, delivery, installation, testing; excludes training and general overheads [1].

items.stem: Explain why IAS 36 requires impaired assets to be written down to their recoverable amount.
items.answer: An asset should not be carried at more than the economic benefits it will generate; writing it down applies prudence and gives a faithful representation of the asset.
items.markingKey: Asset not overstated [1]; prudence/faithful representation [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain two indicators that an asset may be impaired.
items.answer: External: significant fall in market value, adverse changes in technology/market, increased interest rates. Internal: physical damage, obsolescence, worse performance than expected.
items.markingKey: Two indicators [1 each] with explanation [1 each] [4]

items.stem: Odyssey plc bought a machine with a list price of $196,000 less a trade discount of 10%. It also paid: a three-year maintenance contract $1,100, installation $2,900, delivery $5,600. Calculate the cost of the machine to be capitalised under IAS 16.
items.markingKey: Price $196,000 − 10% = $176,400 [1]; include delivery $5,600, installation $2,900 [1]; exclude a three-year maintenance contract (expensed) [1]; cost = $184,900 [1]

items.stem: Banyan Ltd bought a machine with a list price of $137,000 less a trade discount of 10%. It also paid: a three-year maintenance contract $1,900, import duty $10,100, general administration overheads apportioned $900, delivery $1,100, installation $6,100. Calculate the cost of the machine to be capitalised under IAS 16.
items.markingKey: Price $137,000 − 10% = $123,300 [1]; include import duty $10,100, delivery $1,100, installation $6,100 [1]; exclude general administration overheads apportioned, a three-year maintenance contract (expensed) [1]; cost = $140,600 [1]

items.stem: Pinnacle Ltd bought a machine with a list price of $240,000 less a trade discount of 5%. It also paid: installation $3,600, import duty $6,400, delivery $1,700, a three-year maintenance contract $1,300, general administration overheads apportioned $2,500. Calculate the cost of the machine to be capitalised under IAS 16.
items.markingKey: Price $240,000 − 5% = $228,000 [1]; include delivery $1,700, import duty $6,400, installation $3,600 [1]; exclude a three-year maintenance contract, general administration overheads apportioned (expensed) [1]; cost = $239,700 [1]

items.stem: Galaxy Ltd bought a printing press for $157,000 with an estimated residual value of $2,000 and a useful life of 8 years (straight-line). After 3 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $75,000; the machine could be sold for $68,000 less selling costs of $3,000. (a) Calculate the impairment loss. (b) Explain why the competitor's new technology is an indicator of impairment.
items.answer: (a) $23,875 (b) It reduces the demand/value of the output and the cash flows the machine can generate, so its recoverable amount may fall below carrying amount.

items.stem: Meridian Ltd bought a packaging machine for $366,000 with an estimated residual value of $3,000 and a useful life of 5 years (straight-line). After 2 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $167,000; the machine could be sold for $165,000 less selling costs of $2,000. (a) Calculate the depreciation charge for each remaining year after the impairment. (b) Discuss the effect of the impairment on the company's reported profit and return on capital employed.
items.answer: (a) $54,667 (b) Profit falls by $53,800 this year (expense); capital employed falls, so future ROCE may rise as depreciation is lower.
items.markingKey: (a) ($167,000 − $3,000) / 3 = $54,667 [2] (b) Profit effect with figure [1]; capital employed effect [1]; future years [1] [3]

items.stem: Complete the statement: Under IAS 36, the recoverable amount of an asset is …
options: the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use
the lower of cost and net realisable value
items.answer: the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use
items.markingKey: Recoverable amount = max(FV − costs of disposal, VIU) [1].

items.stem: Complete the statement: An asset is impaired when …
options: its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount
items.answer: its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount
items.markingKey: Impairment loss = carrying amount − recoverable amount [1].

items.stem: Explain why the residual value and useful life of assets must be reviewed at least annually under IAS 16.
items.answer: Expectations change; reviewing ensures the depreciation charge reflects the pattern of use of the asset; changes are accounted for prospectively as a change in estimate (IAS 8).
items.markingKey: Estimates change [1]; accurate depreciation/matching [1]; prospective change of estimate [1] [3]

items.stem: Sirocco plc bought a machine with a list price of $197,000. It also paid: delivery $5,800, general administration overheads apportioned $5,400, import duty $6,500. What is the cost of the machine to be capitalised under IAS 16.
items.markingKey: include delivery $5,800, import duty $6,500 [1]; exclude general administration overheads apportioned (expensed) [1]; cost = $209,300 [1]

items.stem: Tamarind Ltd bought a refrigeration unit for $359,000 with an estimated residual value of $5,000 and a useful life of 4 years (straight-line). After 3 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $79,000; the machine could be sold for $73,000 less selling costs of $500. (a) Calculate the annual depreciation and the carrying amount before the impairment review. (b) Explain why the competitor's new technology is an indicator of impairment.
items.answer: (a) $88,500; $93,500 (b) It reduces the demand/value of the output and the cash flows the machine can generate, so its recoverable amount may fall below carrying amount.

items.stem: Complete the statement: Under IAS 2, inventories are valued at …
options: the higher of cost and net realisable value
the lower of cost and net realisable value
items.answer: the lower of cost and net realisable value
items.markingKey: IAS 2: lower of cost and NRV, item by item [1].

items.stem: Explain why IAS 2 requires inventory to be valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
items.answer: Prudence: assets should not be overstated; a loss expected on sale is recognised immediately, while profits are recognised only when realised.
items.markingKey: Prudence/no overstatement [1]; losses recognised when foreseen [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between a change in accounting policy and a change in accounting estimate under IAS 8, giving an example of each.
items.answer: Policy: change in the principles/bases used, e.g. FIFO to weighted average, applied retrospectively. Estimate: revised judgement, e.g. useful life or allowance for receivables, applied prospectively.
items.markingKey: Policy defined + example [1]; estimate defined + example [1]; retrospective vs prospective [1] [3]

items.stem: Condor Ltd holds the following inventory at the year end — Line A: cost $12,200, selling price $16,900; Model Q: cost $29,900, selling price $28,600. Calculate the value of inventory under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV item by item: Line A $12,200, Model Q $28,600 [1]; total $40,800 [1]

items.stem: Banyan Ltd holds the following inventory at the year end — Line C: cost $17,300, selling price $19,200, selling costs $1,700; Batch 7: cost $10,200, selling price $11,900, selling costs $200; Line B: cost $26,600, selling price $35,000, selling costs $800. Calculate the value of inventory under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV item by item: Line C $17,300, Batch 7 $10,200, Line B $26,600 [2]; total $54,100 [1]

items.stem: The draft profit of Galaxy Ltd for the year is $242,000 and closing inventory is $189,000. The auditors find: (1) inventory includes goods at cost $10,000 with NRV of $8,500; (2) purchases of $15,000 for the current year were omitted from the records in error; (3) the directors have revised the useful life of machinery, so the depreciation charge for this year should be $7,500 instead of the $13,000 included. (a) State and explain how IAS 8 classifies item (3). (b) Explain why the directors may be reluctant to accept these adjustments.
items.answer: (a) Change in accounting estimate: applied prospectively from the current year, no restatement of prior years. (b) They reduce reported profit, which may affect bonuses, share price and dividends; however the standards require faithful representation.
items.markingKey: (a) Classification [1]; prospective treatment [1] [2] (b) Motive [1]; ethical/standards point [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain when a company may change an accounting policy under IAS 8.
items.answer: Only if required by a standard or if the change gives more reliable and relevant information; otherwise policies must be applied consistently.
items.markingKey: Required by IFRS [1]; more relevant/reliable [1] [2]

items.stem: Equinox plc bought equipment for $215,000, depreciated straight-line over 5 years. At the start of year 4 the directors estimate the remaining useful life to be 4 years. Explain how IAS 8 applies and calculate the depreciation charge for year 4.
items.answer: Change in accounting estimate — prospective, no restatement. Year 4 charge $21,500
items.markingKey: Change in estimate, prospective [1]; carrying amount after 3 years $86,000 [1]; ($86,000 − $0) / 4 = $21,500 [1]

items.stem: Quetzal plc holds the following inventory at the year end — Model Q: cost $27,600, selling price $21,200, selling costs $600; Line B: cost $5,300, selling price $6,100, selling costs $2,400; Model P: cost $6,800, selling price $9,800, selling costs $500; Model R: cost $11,800, selling price $9,000, selling costs $2,400. Calculate the value of inventory under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV item by item: Model Q $20,600, Line B $3,700, Model P $6,800, Model R $6,600 [3]; total $37,700 [1]

items.stem: Complete the statement: Under IAS 37 a provision is recognised when there is a present obligation, a probable outflow of resources and …
options: a reliable estimate of the amount
items.answer: a reliable estimate of the amount
items.markingKey: All three conditions required [1].

items.stem: Distinguish between a provision and a contingent liability.
items.answer: A provision is a liability of uncertain timing or amount that is probable and can be measured reliably, so it is recognised; a contingent liability is only possible (or cannot be measured), so it is disclosed only.
items.markingKey: Provision: probable, reliable, recognised [1]; contingent liability: possible, disclosed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why non-adjusting events should be disclosed even though they do not change the figures.
items.answer: Material events after the year end could influence users' decisions; without disclosure users would be misled about the company's current position.
items.markingKey: Material to decisions [1]; avoids misleading users [1] [2]

items.stem: The draft profit of Kestrel plc for the year ended 31 December 2025 is $369,000. Before the financial statements were authorised: (1) a court case outstanding at the year end was settled, the company paying damages of $23,500; (2) the company announced a plan to close a division, costing $36,000. Calculate the revised profit, stating whether each event is adjusting or non-adjusting.
items.answer: Revised profit $345,500
items.markingKey: "a court case outstanding at the year end was settled, the company paying damages of $23,500" adjusting: −$23,500; "the company announced a plan to close a division, costing $36,000" non-adjusting: disclose only [1 each]; revised profit $345,500 [1]

items.stem: The draft profit of Equinox plc for the year ended 31 March 2026 is $200,000. Before the financial statements were authorised: (1) the company issued new shares raising $19,000; (2) a fire destroyed a warehouse valued at $31,000; (3) a major customer, owing $28,500 at the year end, was declared bankrupt. Calculate the revised profit, stating whether each event is adjusting or non-adjusting.
items.answer: Revised profit $171,500
items.markingKey: "the company issued new shares raising $19,000" non-adjusting: disclose only; "a fire destroyed a warehouse valued at $31,000" non-adjusting: disclose only; "a major customer, owing $28,500 at the year end, was declared bankrupt" adjusting: −$28,500 [1 each]; revised profit $171,500 [1]

items.stem: Horizon plc has a draft profit of $619,000, current assets $162,000 and current liabilities $151,000 at its year end. After the year end: a customer owing $13,000 at the year end went into liquidation; a flood destroyed inventory bought after the year end costing $100,000. At the year end a former employee was claiming $22,000 for unfair dismissal; lawyers think the claim will probably succeed. (a) Explain how the flood should be reported. (b) Discuss whether the directors should be allowed to omit the provision because "the case has not been decided yet".
items.answer: (a) Non-adjusting event: disclose nature and estimated financial effect in a note if material; no change to figures. (b) No: a present obligation from a past event exists, outflow is probable and estimable, so IAS 37 requires a provision; omitting it overstates profit and misleads users.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) IAS 37 criteria applied [2]; consequence for users/ethics [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a company cannot create a provision for future operating losses.
items.answer: There is no present obligation arising from a past event; future losses relate to future activity, so IAS 37 prohibits a provision.
items.markingKey: No present obligation [1]; no past event [1] [2]

items.stem: At the year end, Saffron plc faces the following: (1) the company plans to refurbish its offices next year at a cost of $17,000; (2) a law requires the company to clean up land it has already contaminated, estimated at $16,000. Apply IAS 37 to each and calculate the total provision to be recognised.
items.answer: (1) no provision (no present obligation); (2) provision. Total provision $16,000
items.markingKey: (1) no provision (no present obligation); (2) provision [1 each]; total provision $16,000 [1]

items.stem: Marula plc has a draft profit of $544,000, current assets $137,000 and current liabilities $214,000 at its year end. After the year end: a customer owing $12,000 at the year end went into liquidation; a flood destroyed inventory bought after the year end costing $53,000. At the year end a former employee was claiming $37,000 for unfair dismissal; lawyers think the claim will probably succeed. (a) Calculate the current ratio before and after the adjustments. (b) Explain how the flood should be reported.
items.answer: (a) 0.64:1 → 0.50:1 (b) Non-adjusting event: disclose nature and estimated financial effect in a note if material; no change to figures.

items.stem: Complete the statement: Under IAS 38, research expenditure must be …
options: added to the cost of inventory
written off as an expense when incurred
items.answer: written off as an expense when incurred
items.markingKey: Research: expense; development: capitalise if criteria met [1].

items.stem: Explain why internally generated brands cannot be recognised as assets under IAS 38.
items.answer: Their cost cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole and cannot be measured reliably.
items.markingKey: Cost not separable from business development [1]; not reliably measurable [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between research and development expenditure.
items.answer: Research is original investigation to gain new knowledge with uncertain outcome; development applies that knowledge to produce new or improved products before commercial production.
items.markingKey: Research defined [1]; development defined [1] [2]

items.stem: Nimbus plc spent $99,000 on research into a new vaccine and $179,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $99,000; capitalised $179,000
items.markingKey: Research $99,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $179,000 [1]

items.stem: Osprey Ltd spent $138,000 on research into a new vaccine and $128,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. A further $140,000 of development was spent before technical feasibility was demonstrated. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $278,000; capitalised $128,000
items.markingKey: Research $138,000 expensed [1]; pre-feasibility development $140,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $128,000 [1]

items.stem: Sunbird plc has a draft profit of $477,000. The directors have capitalised: research costs $199,000, development costs meeting all IAS 38 criteria $353,000, a patent bought during the year for $44,000 (legal life 10 years, full year's amortisation), and an internally generated brand valued by the marketing director at $310,000 (credited to profit). (a) Explain why the brand cannot be recognised. (b) Discuss the ethical issues raised by the directors' treatment.
items.answer: (a) It is internally generated; its cost cannot be separated from the cost of running the business and its value is not reliably measurable. (b) Overstating profit and assets misleads shareholders and lenders; may be motivated by bonuses; breaches integrity/objectivity; auditors should insist on correction.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) Two issues [2]; consequence [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why capitalising development costs can improve reported profit in the short term.
items.answer: Costs go to the statement of financial position rather than the income statement, so current expenses fall; the cost is charged later as amortisation.
items.markingKey: Expense deferred [1]; amortised later (matching) [1] [2]

items.stem: Marula plc spent $88,000 on research into a new vaccine and $143,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. A further $32,000 of development was spent before technical feasibility was demonstrated. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $120,000; capitalised $143,000
items.markingKey: Research $88,000 expensed [1]; pre-feasibility development $32,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $143,000 [1]

items.stem: Marula plc has a draft profit of $417,000. The directors have capitalised: research costs $164,000, development costs meeting all IAS 38 criteria $305,000, a patent bought during the year for $88,000 (legal life 15 years, full year's amortisation), and an internally generated brand valued by the marketing director at $480,000 (credited to profit). (a) Calculate the intangible assets to be shown in the statement of financial position. (b) Explain why the brand cannot be recognised.
items.answer: (a) $387,133 (b) It is internally generated; its cost cannot be separated from the cost of running the business and its value is not reliably measurable.

items.stem: Complete the statement: When an item of PPE is revalued upwards, the gain is credited to …
options: retained earnings directly as realised profit
items.answer: a revaluation surplus (reserve) in equity
items.markingKey: IAS 16: surplus to OCI/revaluation reserve [1].

items.stem: When Saffron plc bought new equipment, the accountant capitalised staff training of $1,000 and charged installation costs of $2,000 to the income statement. Explain the errors and their net effect on the carrying amount of the equipment.
items.answer: Training is not a cost of bringing the asset to working condition and must be expensed; installation is directly attributable and must be capitalised. The asset is understated by $1,000.
items.markingKey: Training expensed (IAS 16) [1]; installation capitalised [1]; net effect $1,000 understated [1] [3]

items.stem: Sunbird plc owns a delivery fleet with a carrying amount of $312,000. It could be sold for $316,000 with selling costs of $5,000. The present value of the future cash flows from using it is $312,000. Calculate the recoverable amount and any impairment loss.
items.answer: Recoverable amount $312,000; impairment loss $0
items.markingKey: FV less costs = $311,000; VIU $312,000; recoverable $312,000 ≥ carrying amount, so no impairment [2]

items.stem: Sirocco plc bought a CNC lathe for $339,000 with an estimated residual value of $18,000 and a useful life of 5 years (straight-line). After 2 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $112,000; the machine could be sold for $105,000 less selling costs of $3,000. (a) Calculate the depreciation charge for each remaining year after the impairment. (b) Explain why the competitor's new technology is an indicator of impairment.
items.answer: (a) $31,333 (b) It reduces the demand/value of the output and the cash flows the machine can generate, so its recoverable amount may fall below carrying amount.

items.stem: Lynx Ltd bought a packaging machine for $230,000 with an estimated residual value of $9,000 and a useful life of 10 years (straight-line). After 2 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $98,000; the machine could be sold for $90,000 less selling costs of $1,000. (a) Calculate the annual depreciation and the carrying amount before the impairment review. (b) Explain why the competitor's new technology is an indicator of impairment.
items.answer: (a) $22,100; $185,800 (b) It reduces the demand/value of the output and the cash flows the machine can generate, so its recoverable amount may fall below carrying amount.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Complete the statement: Under IAS 8 a change in the estimated useful life of a machine is … (b) Which of these costs may be included in the cost of inventory under IAS 2?
items.answer: (a) a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively (b) Carriage inwards
items.markingKey: (a) Estimates: prospective; policies and errors: retrospective [1]. (b) Purchase costs, conversion costs, costs to bring to present location [1].

items.stem: Meridian Ltd valued damaged goods at their cost of $40,000. They can be sold for $36,500 after repair costs of $400. Explain the error and its effect on profit.
items.answer: IAS 2 requires the lower of cost and NRV. NRV = $36,100, so inventory should be $36,100. Inventory and profit are overstated by $3,900.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV [1]; NRV $36,500 − $400 = $36,100 [1]; profit overstated by $3,900 [1] [3]

items.stem: Saffron plc holds the following inventory at the year end — Model P: cost $10,000, selling price $12,600; Line C: cost $4,800, selling price $6,200. Calculate the value of inventory under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV item by item: Model P $10,000, Line C $4,800 [1]; total $14,800 [1]

items.stem: The draft profit of Nimbus plc for the year is $290,000 and closing inventory is $199,000. The auditors find: (1) inventory includes goods at cost $24,500 with NRV of $20,000; (2) purchases of $2,000 for the current year were omitted from the records in error; (3) the directors have revised the useful life of machinery, so the depreciation charge for this year should be $6,500 instead of the $12,000 included. (a) Calculate the revised profit for the year. (b) Calculate the revised closing inventory.

Two weeks after the year end of Galaxy Ltd, a court case outstanding at the year end was settled, the company paying damages of $30,000. State whether this is an adjusting or non-adjusting event under IAS 10 and explain how it is treated.
items.answer: Adjusting: confirms an obligation that existed at the year end. The figures are amended.
items.markingKey: adjusting [1]; reason: confirms an obligation that existed at the year end [1]; treatment [1] [3]

items.stem: Two weeks after the year end of Quetzal plc, a major customer, owing $27,000 at the year end, was declared bankrupt. State whether this is an adjusting or non-adjusting event under IAS 10 and explain how it is treated.
items.answer: Adjusting: provides evidence of conditions at the year end (receivable was irrecoverable). The figures are amended.
items.markingKey: adjusting [1]; reason: provides evidence of conditions at the year end (receivable was irrecoverable) [1]; treatment [1] [3]

items.stem: The draft profit of Lynx Ltd for the year ended 30 June 2026 is $313,000. Before the financial statements were authorised: (1) a fire destroyed a warehouse valued at $16,500; (2) inventory held at the year end at cost of $37,500 was sold for $2,000 less than cost. Calculate the revised profit, stating whether each event is adjusting or non-adjusting.
items.answer: Revised profit $311,000
items.markingKey: "a fire destroyed a warehouse valued at $16,500" non-adjusting: disclose only; "inventory held at the year end at cost of $37,500 was sold for $2,000 less than cost" adjusting: −$2,000 [1 each]; revised profit $311,000 [1]

items.stem: The accountant of Kestrel plc capitalised $53,000 spent on research into a new material, arguing that "it will definitely lead to profitable products". Explain why this treatment is wrong and its effect on the financial statements.
items.answer: Research outcomes are uncertain, so IAS 38 requires research to be expensed. Profit and intangible assets are overstated by $53,000.
items.markingKey: Research must be expensed [1]; future benefits not demonstrable [1]; profit/assets overstated $53,000 [1] [3]

items.stem: Meridian Ltd spent $123,000 on research into an electric scooter battery and $95,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $123,000; capitalised $95,000
items.markingKey: Research $123,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $95,000 [1]

items.stem: Meridian Ltd spent $58,000 on research into a mobile banking app and $49,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. A further $117,000 of development was spent before technical feasibility was demonstrated. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $175,000; capitalised $49,000
items.markingKey: Research $58,000 expensed [1]; pre-feasibility development $117,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $49,000 [1]

items.stem: Complete the statement: Depreciation under IAS 16 is defined as …
options: a fund of cash set aside to replace assets
a fall in the market value of an asset
the amount for which an asset could be sold
the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life
items.answer: the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life
items.markingKey: Depreciable amount = cost − residual value, allocated over useful life [1].

items.stem: When Delta Ltd bought new equipment, the accountant capitalised staff training of $1,500 and charged installation costs of $5,000 to the income statement. Explain the errors and their net effect on the carrying amount of the equipment.
items.answer: Training is not a cost of bringing the asset to working condition and must be expensed; installation is directly attributable and must be capitalised. The asset is understated by $3,500.
items.markingKey: Training expensed (IAS 16) [1]; installation capitalised [1]; net effect $3,500 understated [1] [3]

items.stem: Kauri Ltd owns a specialist printing press with a carrying amount of $336,000. It could be sold for $355,000 with selling costs of $9,000. The present value of the future cash flows from using it is $329,000. Calculate the recoverable amount and any impairment loss.
items.answer: Recoverable amount $346,000; impairment loss $0
items.markingKey: FV less costs = $346,000; VIU $329,000; recoverable $346,000 ≥ carrying amount, so no impairment [2]

items.stem: Marula plc bought a printing press for $232,000 with an estimated residual value of $4,000 and a useful life of 8 years (straight-line). After 2 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $146,000; the machine could be sold for $139,000 less selling costs of $1,500. (a) Calculate the annual depreciation and the carrying amount before the impairment review. (b) Calculate the impairment loss.

Osprey Ltd bought a refrigeration unit for $220,000 with an estimated residual value of $3,000 and a useful life of 10 years (straight-line). After 2 years, a competitor launches a cheaper technology. The value in use is now estimated at $92,000; the machine could be sold for $82,000 less selling costs of $500. (a) Calculate the impairment loss. (b) Calculate the depreciation charge for each remaining year after the impairment.
Answer both parts. (a) Complete the statement: Under IAS 8, a material prior period error is corrected … (b) Complete the statement: Under IAS 2, inventories are valued at …
items.answer: (a) retrospectively, by restating the comparative figures (b) the lower of cost and net realisable value
items.markingKey: (a) Errors restated retrospectively [1]. (b) IAS 2: lower of cost and NRV, item by item [1].

items.stem: Cobalt Ltd valued damaged goods at their cost of $28,500. They can be sold for $26,500 after repair costs of $800. Explain the error and its effect on profit.
items.answer: IAS 2 requires the lower of cost and NRV. NRV = $25,700, so inventory should be $25,700. Inventory and profit are overstated by $2,800.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV [1]; NRV $26,500 − $800 = $25,700 [1]; profit overstated by $2,800 [1] [3]

items.stem: Tamarind Ltd holds the following inventory at the year end — Line B: cost $25,500, selling price $31,400; Batch 7: cost $11,100, selling price $10,400. Calculate the value of inventory under IAS 2.
items.markingKey: Lower of cost and NRV item by item: Line B $25,500, Batch 7 $10,400 [1]; total $35,900 [1]

items.stem: The draft profit of Sunbird plc for the year is $388,000 and closing inventory is $186,000. The auditors find: (1) inventory includes goods at cost $20,000 with NRV of $15,500; (2) purchases of $13,000 for the current year were omitted from the records in error; (3) the directors have revised the useful life of machinery, so the depreciation charge for this year should be $5,000 instead of the $10,500 included. (a) Calculate the revised closing inventory. (b) State and explain how IAS 8 classifies item (3). (c) Explain why the directors may be reluctant to accept these adjustments.
items.answer: (a) $181,500 (b) Change in accounting estimate: applied prospectively from the current year, no restatement of prior years. (c) They reduce reported profit, which may affect bonuses, share price and dividends; however the standards require faithful representation.
items.markingKey: (a) $186,000 − $4,500 = $181,500 [1] (b) Classification [1]; prospective treatment [1] [2] (c) Motive [1]; ethical/standards point [1] [2]

items.stem: Two weeks after the year end of Banyan Ltd, the company announced a plan to close a division, costing $59,000. State whether this is an adjusting or non-adjusting event under IAS 10 and explain how it is treated.
items.answer: Non-adjusting: decision taken after the year end; disclose. The financial statements are not adjusted.
items.markingKey: non-adjusting [1]; reason: decision taken after the year end; disclose [1]; treatment [1] [3]

items.stem: Two weeks after the year end of Tamarind Ltd, a major customer, owing $13,000 at the year end, was declared bankrupt. State whether this is an adjusting or non-adjusting event under IAS 10 and explain how it is treated.
items.answer: Adjusting: provides evidence of conditions at the year end (receivable was irrecoverable). The figures are amended.
items.markingKey: adjusting [1]; reason: provides evidence of conditions at the year end (receivable was irrecoverable) [1]; treatment [1] [3]

items.stem: At the year end, Lynx Ltd faces the following: (1) the company plans to refurbish its offices next year at a cost of $37,000; (2) a customer is suing for $61,000; lawyers advise the company will probably lose. Apply IAS 37 to each and calculate the total provision to be recognised.
items.answer: (1) no provision (no present obligation); (2) provision. Total provision $61,000
items.markingKey: (1) no provision (no present obligation); (2) provision [1 each]; total provision $61,000 [1]

items.stem: The accountant of Ibis plc capitalised $89,000 spent on research into a new material, arguing that "it will definitely lead to profitable products". Explain why this treatment is wrong and its effect on the financial statements.
items.answer: Research outcomes are uncertain, so IAS 38 requires research to be expensed. Profit and intangible assets are overstated by $89,000.
items.markingKey: Research must be expensed [1]; future benefits not demonstrable [1]; profit/assets overstated $89,000 [1] [3]

items.stem: Lynx Ltd spent $97,000 on research into a mobile banking app and $126,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $97,000; capitalised $126,000
items.markingKey: Research $97,000 expensed [1]; capitalise $126,000 [1]

items.stem: Cobalt Ltd spent $113,000 on research into a drought-resistant seed and $97,000 on development after all IAS 38 criteria were met. A further $79,000 of development was spent before technical feasibility was demonstrated. Calculate the amount charged as an expense and the amount capitalised.
items.answer: Expense $192,000; capitalised $97,000
